at vaske.explanation: "At vaske" means to wash, for clothes, dishes, your hands or the car. "Jeg vasker tøj" means "I wash clothes". With your body you say "vaske sig" (wash yourself). "At vaske op" means to do the dishes, and "at vaske tøj" means to do the laundry.

sentence.en: I wash clothes every Sunday.

at vaske op.explanation: "At vaske op" means to do the dishes by hand. The little word "op" belongs to the verb and stays after it: "Jeg vasker op." Do not mix it up with "at vaske" (to wash), which is for clothes, hands or the car. The pile of dirty dishes is called "opvasken".

sentence.en: I do the dishes after dinner.

at vaske sig.explanation: "At vaske sig" means to wash yourself. The little word "sig" means 'oneself', and it changes to "mig" when you talk about yourself: "jeg vasker mig". If you wash something else, you drop it: "at vaske hænder" or "at vaske tøj".

sentence.en: I wash myself every morning.

at veje.explanation: "At veje" works in two ways, just like in English: you can weigh something ("Jeg vejer pakken") or you can weigh a certain amount ("Jeg vejer 70 kilo"). The word for a scale, and for weight, is "en vægt".

sentence.en: Can you weigh the package for me?

at vente.explanation: "At vente" means to wait: "Jeg venter på bussen" (I am waiting for the bus). You "vente på" something, which means wait for it. A useful phrase is "Vent lidt" (Wait a moment). It also means to expect: "Hun venter barn" means She is expecting a baby.

sentence.en: I am waiting for the bus.

at vente på.explanation: "At vente på" means to wait for someone or something. In Danish you need "på" (on), where English says 'for'. So it is "Jeg venter på bussen" (I'm waiting for the bus). A simple "Vent!" means 'Wait!'.

sentence.en: I am waiting for the bus.

at vide.explanation: "At vide" means to know a fact, as in "Jeg ved det" (I know it) or "Jeg ved ikke" (I don't know). Danish has a second word, "at kende", for knowing a person or a place. A tip: "Jeg ved det ikke" is the usual way to say I don't know. The form "ved" is the same for every person.

sentence.en: I don't know where he is.

at ville.explanation: "At ville" means to want to, and it can also say that something will happen. "Jeg vil have en kop kaffe" means I want a cup of coffee, and a polite way to ask for something. It is followed straight by another action word, with no "at". Note that "vil" is not just "will": it is about wanting, so use "skal" for plans and duties.

sentence.da: Jeg **vil** gerne have en kop te.
sentence.en: I would like a cup of tea.

at vinde.explanation: "At vinde" means to win: "Vi vinder kampen" (We win the match). You can win a game, a prize or a race. The opposite is "at tabe" (to lose). The past form "vandt" and the "have done" form "vundet" are irregular. A winner is "en vinder", and "en gevinst" is a prize you win.

sentence.en: We are winning the match today.

at vise.explanation: "At vise" means to show: "Jeg viser dig vej" (I show you the way). You show something to someone, so the person comes first without "til": "Hun viser mig bogen". A handy phrase is "Vis mig" (Show me). It is also used when a clock or a meter shows something.

sentence.en: Can you show me the way?

at vågne.explanation: "At vågne" means to wake up by yourself, as in "Jeg vågner klokken syv" (I wake up at seven). When someone else wakes you, Danish says "at vække". A related phrase is "at stå op" (to get up). Note that for the "have done" form, Danish uses "er" here: "Jeg er vågnet".

sentence.en: I wake up early every day.

at vågne op.explanation: "At vågne op" means to wake up, meaning the moment you become awake. Often people just say "at vågne" and the "op" is optional. Don't mix it up with "at stå op", which means getting out of bed.

sentence.en: I wake up at seven o'clock.

at vælge.explanation: "At vælge" means to choose or to pick. "Jeg vælger den røde" means "I choose the red one". The past form "valgte" and the "have" form "valgt" are irregular, so learn them as they are. The act of choosing is "et valg" (a choice), which is also the word for an election.

sentence.en: You may choose a colour.

at være.explanation: "At være" means to be, and it is the most important word in Danish. It is used for describing people and things ("Jeg er træt"), for saying where something is, and for saying what someone is. Its forms are very irregular, so learn "er", "var" and "været" by heart. Unlike English, Danish uses the same form "er" for I, you, he, we and they.

sentence.en: I am at home today.

at være syg.explanation: "At være syg" means to be sick or ill. You use it to describe the state of being unwell: "Jeg er syg" (I am sick). It covers anything from a cold to a serious illness. To get sick, say "at blive syg". The way to tell work you can't come is "at melde sig syg".

sentence.en: My son is sick today.

at være væk.explanation: "At være væk" means to be gone or to be away. It is used for people who are not there ("Han er væk") and for things that have disappeared ("Min nøgle er væk"). It describes the state of being gone, not the act of leaving.

sentence.en: My key is gone.

en vaccine.explanation: "Vaccine" is borrowed from Latin and looks almost like the English word, but the stress falls on the middle: vak-SEE-ne. The matching verb is "at vaccinere" (to vaccinate), and the act of getting it is "en vaccination". Denmark has a national vaccination programme for children, which people often just call "børnevaccinationsprogrammet".

sentence.en: She got a vaccine yesterday.

en vegetar.explanation: "En vegetar" is a person who does not eat meat. Use it to say what you are: "Jeg er vegetar". The word that describes food is "vegetarisk", for example "en vegetarisk ret" (a vegetarian dish).

sentence.da: Jeg er **vegetar**, så jeg spiser ikke kød.
sentence.en: I am a vegetarian, so I do not eat meat.

en vej.explanation: "En vej" means a road or a way. It is used for roads and also for a route you take: "at spørge om vej" means to ask for directions. Street names in Denmark often end in "-vej", like "Strandvejen". In Danish, 'the road' is "vejen".

sentence.en: Which way should I go?

en vejrudsigt.explanation: "En vejrudsigt" is a weather forecast, a description of what the weather will be like. It is built from "vejr" (weather) and "udsigt" (outlook). You can check it on TV, on the radio or on your phone.

sentence.en: What does the weather forecast say for tomorrow?

en ven.explanation: "En ven" is a male friend or a friend in general. The plural is "venner". A female friend is "en veninde". Be careful with "kæreste", which is a boyfriend or girlfriend, not just a friend. "Min bedste ven" is my best friend.

sentence.en: He is my best friend.

en veninde.explanation: "En veninde" is a female friend. Danish has a separate word for a man's or boy's friend: "en ven". The word "veninde" is used for a woman's friend or a girl's friend. It is regular, and the plural is "veninder".

sentence.en: I am going out with my friend.

en verden.explanation: "En verden" means a world, and with 'the' it is "verdenen", often 'the whole world'. You'll hear it in phrases like "i hele verden" (all over the world). And the word "verdens" is used for 'the world's' like "verdens bedste" (the best in the world).

sentence.en: She travels around the world.

en vin.explanation: "En vin" is a wine. Usually you say the colour: "en rødvin" (red) or "en hvidvin" (white). In a restaurant you can order "et glas vin" (a glass of wine) or "en flaske vin" (a bottle of wine).

sentence.da: Vi bestiller en flaske **vin** til maden.
sentence.en: We order a bottle of wine for the meal.

en vinter.explanation: En vinter is a winter. In Danish, "the winter" is "vinteren", and the more-than-one form is "vintre", where the e before the r drops out. Use "om vinteren" for "in the winter" in general, and "i vinter" for this winter. Danish winters are dark and often grey, which is why Danes love candles.

sentence.en: It gets dark early in the winter.

en vinterjakke.explanation: "En vinterjakke" is a warm jacket for winter. It is built from "vinter" (winter) and "jakke" (jacket). Danish winters are cold, wet and windy, so a good one is important. You can put other words in front of "jakke" in the same way, like "regnjakke" (rain jacket).

sentence.en: I need a new winter jacket.

en væg.explanation: "En væg" means a wall, such as a wall inside a room. In Danish, 'the wall' is "væggen" and the plural is "vægge". Notice the double 'g' in the forms with an ending. A big outer wall, such as a garden wall, can also be "en mur".

sentence.en: A picture is hanging on the wall.

et vandrerhjem.explanation: "Vandrerhjem" is a hostel, a cheap place to stay, and it literally means "a hiker's home". Denmark has many of them, and some are very good for families. The plural has the same form, with the double m when "the" is added: "vandrerhjemmet".

sentence.en: We are staying at a hostel.

et venteværelse.explanation: "Et venteværelse" is a waiting room, such as at the doctor or dentist. It is built from "vente" (wait) and "værelse" (room). "Sid i venteværelset" means "sit in the waiting room" and is what the receptionist may say to you.

sentence.en: We are sitting in the waiting room.

et vindue.explanation: "Et vindue" means a window. In Danish, 'the window' is "vinduet" and the plural is "vinduer". You can say "at åbne vinduet" (to open the window). The ending sounds a bit like 'dew', so say it softly.

sentence.en: There is a window in the kitchen.

et visum.explanation: "Visum" is a visa, the permission to enter or live in a country. And the plural "visa" is a Latin-style form that looks different from the single word. Use it with "at søge om" (to apply for): "Jeg søger om et visum."

sentence.en: I need a visa.

et værelse.explanation: "Et værelse" is a room, in a home or in a hotel. At a hotel you book "et værelse" for the night. The word means a room in the sense of a space to live or sleep in, and not room as in space (that is "plads").

sentence.da: Jeg har booket et **værelse** til to nætter.
sentence.en: I have booked a room for two nights.

vand.explanation: Vand is water. It is an et-word, so "the water" is "vandet". You use it without "et" when you mean water in general, as in "Jeg drikker vand" (I drink water). To ask for some in a restaurant, say "Må jeg få et glas vand?". Tap water is safe to drink in Denmark, and "koldt vand" means cold water.

sentence.da: Må jeg bede om et glas **vand**?
sentence.en: May I have a glass of water?

varm.explanation: "Varm" means warm or hot, for weather, food, drinks and rooms. Danish does not have separate everyday words for warm and hot like English does; "varm" covers both, and for very hot weather people say "meget varmt" or "hedt". You add "t" for et-words ("et varmt værelse"). The opposite is "kold" (cold).

sentence.en: The coffee is still hot.

varme.explanation: "Varme" as an en-word means heat or warmth. "Varmen" is "the heat", for example on a hot summer day. It looks like the verb "at varme" (to warm) and the plural word "varme" (warm), so the context tells you which one it is. The opposite is "kulde".

sentence.da: **Varmen** er svær at holde ud i dag.
sentence.en: The heat is hard to bear today.

ved.explanation: "Ved" means by or at, and it shows something is close to or next to something else: "ved vinduet". Careful: "ved" is also the "I know" form of "at vide": "Jeg ved det". The meaning is clear from the sentence.

sentence.en: He is sitting by the window.

ved siden af.explanation: "Ved siden af" means "next to" or "beside". It is made of three small words and is often used to tell where things are, like "Banken ligger ved siden af posthuset" (The bank is next to the post office). You can also say "lige ved siden af" for "right next to". It can also mean "alongside", as in "ved siden af mit arbejde" (alongside my job).

sentence.en: The bank is next to the post office.

vegetarisk.explanation: "Vegetarisk" means vegetarian, so without meat, and you use it to describe food. The form for an et-word is the same, "vegetarisk", with no "t" added; the plural adds "e": "vegetariske". You can ask "Har I noget vegetarisk?" (Do you have anything vegetarian?).

sentence.en: Do you have a vegetarian dish?

vejr.explanation: Vejr is the weather. It is an et-word, so you never say "a weather", and "the weather" is "vejret". Weather is a favourite topic of small talk in Denmark. A good question is "Hvordan er vejret?" (How is the weather?), and you can answer with "Det er godt vejr" or "Det er dårligt vejr". Note that "godt" gets a t because the word is an et-word.

sentence.en: How is the weather today?

forms.en: Thanks for the meal. You're welcome.

velbekomme.explanation: "Velbekomme" is a mealtime word. It can be said while serving food to mean "enjoy", and it is the reply when someone says "tak for mad" afterwards, meaning "you're welcome". It is only used about food and drink. For other thanks, use "selv tak" or "det var så lidt".

sentence.en: Here is the soup. Enjoy!

velkommen.explanation: Means "welcome". Use it when greeting guests, and add "til" plus the place: "velkommen til Danmark". It stays the same for one or many people. Do not use it to mean "you're welcome", which is "selv tak" or "det var så lidt".

sentence.en: Welcome to our home!

venlig.explanation: "Venlig" means friendly or kind, for people, voices and smiles. It is a good word to describe polite and pleasant behaviour. Add "t" for et-words ("et venligt svar") and "-e" for more than one. "Venlig hilsen" (kind regards) is the usual way to end a Danish email. The opposite is "uvenlig" (unfriendly).

sentence.en: Everyone is very friendly here.

venstre.explanation: "Venstre" means left, as in the left side or the left hand. It stays the same whatever word it describes. It is the opposite of "højre" (right). In directions you usually say "til venstre" (to the left).

sentence.en: Take the first road on the left.

vent lidt.explanation: "Vent lidt" means "wait a bit" and is how you ask someone to hold on for a moment. The word "lidt" means "a little", so it softens the request. Add "tak" to be polite. It is also what you say when you need a second to think or find something.

sentence.en: Wait a bit, I'm finding my bag.

vest.explanation: "Vest" means west, one of the four main directions. It is used in names such as "Vestjylland" (western Jutland), which faces the North Sea. The opposite is "øst" (east). In Copenhagen "Vesterbro" is a part of town named after the west.

sentence.en: The sun goes down in the west.

vi.explanation: "Vi" means "we". It always comes first when you are the one doing something, like "Vi bor her". After a verb or word like "to" you use "os" instead: "Han ser os" (He sees us). In questions the verb jumps in front, as in "Skal vi gå?" meaning "Shall we go?".

sentence.en: We are going to the cinema tonight.

vi ses.explanation: "Vi ses" literally means "we are seen" and is the everyday way to say "see you" when parting. Add a time to be specific: "vi ses i morgen" or "vi ses på fredag". It is casual and fine with friends, colleagues and shop staff. Use "på gensyn" in a more formal setting.

sentence.da: Jeg skal gå nu. **Vi ses** i morgen!
sentence.en: I have to go now. See you tomorrow!

vi tales ved.explanation: "Vi tales ved" means "we will talk" and is a friendly goodbye, mostly after a phone call or message, when you expect to speak again soon. It sounds a little like "talk to you soon". Use "vi ses" instead when you expect to meet in person.

sentence.da: Jeg ringer i aften. **Vi tales ved!**
sentence.en: I'll call tonight. Talk soon!

vigtig.explanation: "Vigtig" means important, for things, people, news and decisions. "Det er vigtigt" is a common phrase meaning "It is important". Add "t" for et-words ("et vigtigt møde") and "-e" for more than one. The word "vigtigt" is also used alone like "important": "Det er vigtigt at sove" (It is important to sleep). An opposite is "uvigtig" or "ligegyldig".

sentence.en: It is important to drink water.

vind.explanation: Vind is wind. It is an en-word, so "the wind" is "vinden". To say that it is windy you use the verb "at blæse": "Det blæser". Denmark is quite windy, so people talk about it a lot, and Danish wind turbines are known worldwide. A very strong wind is "en storm" (a storm).

sentence.en: The wind is cold today.

virkelig.explanation: "Virkelig" means "really" and adds strength: "virkelig god" (really good). It can also mean "truly" when you doubt something: "Virkelig?" (Really?). It comes from "virke" (to work / seem). The everyday way to show surprise is just "Nåh, virkelig?".

sentence.en: That was really lovely.

vores.explanation: "Vores" means "our" or "ours". It never changes, so it fits en-words, et-words and many things: "vores hus", "vores bil", "vores venner". It comes from "vi" (we) and "os" (us). It is easy to use because there is only this one form.

sentence.en: Our house is close to the harbour.

vred.explanation: "Vred" means angry. To say you are angry at someone, use "vred på": "Jeg er vred på ham". It is a fairly strong word; for being a little annoyed Danes use "irriteret" or "sur". Add "t" for et-words ("et vredt barn") and "-e" for more than one. The word for anger itself is "vrede", and the opposite feeling is "rolig" (calm).

sentence.en: She is angry with her brother.

våd.explanation: "Våd" means wet, for clothes, hair, the ground, or anything soaked with water. Add "t" for et-words ("et vådt håndklæde") and "-e" for more than one. The opposite is "tør" (dry). Danish weather is often wet, so you will meet this word a lot in talk about rain: "Det er vådt udenfor" (It is wet outside).

sentence.en: My shoes are completely wet.

vågen.explanation: "Vågen" means awake. "Er du vågen?" asks whether someone is awake. The verb "at vågne" means to wake up, as in "Jeg vågnede klokken syv" (I woke up at seven). Add "t" for et-words ("et vågent barn") and the form for more than one drops the "e": "vågne". The opposite is "i søvn" or "søvnig" (sleepy).

sentence.en: I was awake all night.

væk.explanation: "Væk" means "away" or "gone". It is used with verbs of moving or taking: "Gå væk" (Go away) and "Hun løber væk" (She runs away). "Min nøgle er væk" means "My key is gone" or missing. It is quite blunt as an order, so "Gå væk!" can sound rude.

sentence.en: My bag is gone.

værre.explanation: "Værre" means worse. It is the "-er" form of "dårlig" (bad) and never changes its ending. The next step up is "værst" (worst). Use it to compare: "Det er værre end før" means "It is worse than before".

sentence.en: It is worse than before.

forms.en: Here you go, here is your coffee.

værsgo.explanation: "Værsgo" is what you say when you hand someone something or invite them to go ahead. It covers "here you go", "please, help yourself" and "go ahead". The reply is usually "tak". It is not the same as "you're welcome", although Danes sometimes say it that way too when handing over something.

sentence.en: Here you go, here is your ticket.

værst.explanation: "Værst" means worst. It is the top step after "dårlig" (bad) and "værre" (worse). Alone it stays "værst" ("Det er værst"), and before a word it adds an "e": "den værste dag". The opposite is "bedst" (best).

sentence.da: Det var den **værste** dag i mit liv.
sentence.en: It was the worst day of my life.
